title: Error Spotting, Sentence Improvement & Word Usage — Practice (Vol. 2)

questions.question:
Find the segment that contains an error. If there is none, choose "No error".

Neither the manager nor / his two assistants / was present / at the review meeting.
questions.solution: With "neither ... nor", the verb agrees with the nearer subject. The nearer subject "his two assistants" is plural, so it must be "were present."
questions.trick: In neither/nor and either/or, the verb obeys the noun sitting closest to it. Read only the part after "nor."

questions.question:
Find the segment that contains an error. If there is none, choose "No error".

The number of applicants / for the clerical post / have increased / sharply this year.
questions.solution: "The number of + plural noun" takes a singular verb; only "A number of" takes a plural verb. So "has increased."
questions.trick: "THE number" = one figure = singular. "A number of" = many = plural.

questions.question:
Find the segment that contains an error. If there is none, choose "No error".

By the time the auditor arrived, / the staff already / submitted all / the pending vouchers.
options: By the time the auditor arrived,
questions.solution: With "By the time ... arrived" (past), the earlier action needs the past perfect. So "the staff had already submitted."
questions.trick: Two past actions, one earlier — the earlier one takes "had + V3."

questions.question:
Find the segment that contains an error. If there is none, choose "No error".

She has been working / in this branch / since the last five years / without a break.
questions.solution: "Since" marks a point of time; a stretch of time takes "for." So "for the last five years."
questions.trick: SINCE a point (since 2019), FOR a period (for five years).

questions.question:
Find the segment that contains an error. If there is none, choose "No error".

The committee was divided / in their opinion / about whether to / approve the new loan scheme.
questions.solution: "Committee" here acts as a single unit, so use the singular pronoun "its." So "in its opinion."
questions.trick: A collective noun acting as one body = singular (its), not "their."

questions.question:
Find the segment that contains an error. If there is none, choose "No error".

He is one of those officers / who always insists / on verifying every / document personally.
options: He is one of those officers
questions.solution: In "one of those officers who ...", the relative pronoun "who" refers to the plural "officers," so the verb is plural: "who always insist."
questions.trick: "One of those X who" — the verb after "who" is plural because it points to X, not to "one."

questions.question:
Find the segment that contains an error. If there is none, choose "No error".

The teacher distributed / the prizes among / the two toppers / of the class.
questions.solution: "Among" is used for more than two; for exactly two persons use "between." So "the prizes between the two toppers."
questions.trick: BETWEEN for two, AMONG for three or more. The clue word here is "the two."

questions.question:
Find the segment that contains an error. If there is none, choose "No error".

I look forward to / meet you / at the conference / next month.
questions.solution: "Look forward to" ends in a preposition "to," which must be followed by a gerund (-ing), not the base verb. So "look forward to meeting you."
questions.trick: In "look forward to," the "to" is a preposition — always follow it with a verb+ing.

questions.question:
Find the segment that contains an error. If there is none, choose "No error".

Hardly had she entered the hall / than the lights / suddenly went off / across the whole floor.
options: Hardly had she entered the hall
questions.solution: "Hardly ... when" is the correct correlative pair (not "than"). So "Hardly had she entered ... when the lights ..."
questions.trick: Hardly/Scarcely pair with WHEN; No sooner pairs with THAN.

questions.question:
Find the segment that contains an error. If there is none, choose "No error".

There are less / candidates this year / than the branch / had expected.
questions.solution: "Candidates" are countable, so use "fewer," not "less." So "There are fewer candidates."
questions.trick: FEWER for things you can count, LESS for things you measure (less water, fewer bottles).

questions.question:
Find the segment that contains an error. If there is none, choose "No error".

In my opinion, / I think the proposal / deserves a more / careful review.
questions.solution: Redundancy: "In my opinion" and "I think" mean the same thing; using both is repetitive. Drop one.
questions.trick: Watch for double-idea phrases — "In my opinion, I think" says the same thing twice.

questions.question:
Find the segment that contains an error. If there is none, choose "No error".

This year's revenue is / far more higher / than what the / firm reported last year.
questions.solution: Double comparative. "Higher" is already comparative, so "more higher" is wrong. Use "far higher."
questions.trick: Never stack two comparatives: no "more higher," "more better," "most easiest."

questions.question:
Find the segment that contains an error. If there is none, choose "No error".

Each of the trainees / were asked to submit / a report before / leaving the premises.
questions.solution: "Each of the + plural" takes a singular verb. So "was asked to submit."
questions.trick: Each / Every / Either / Neither + noun = always singular verb.

questions.question:
Find the segment that contains an error. If there is none, choose "No error".

The jury have / taken their seats / and are ready / to deliver the verdict.
questions.solution: "Jury" is a collective noun; when members act individually (taking their seats), the plural verb "have" and pronoun "their" are acceptable. The sentence is internally consistent.
questions.trick: Collective noun + members acting separately = plural verb is fine. Consistency is what matters.

questions.question:
Find the segment that contains an error. If there is none, choose "No error".

He congratulated me / for winning / the inter-bank / debate competition.
questions.solution: The correct preposition is "congratulate someone ON something." So "congratulated me on winning."
questions.trick: Congratulate ON, not "for."

questions.question:
Find the segment that contains an error. If there is none, choose "No error".

Not only the director / but also the shareholders / was unhappy with / the quarterly results.
questions.solution: "Not only ... but also" — the verb agrees with the nearer subject "the shareholders" (plural). So "were unhappy."
questions.trick: Like neither/nor, the "not only ... but also" verb follows the nearest subject.

questions.question:
Find the segment that contains an error. If there is none, choose "No error".

A honest officer / is respected by / everyone in the / entire department.
questions.solution: "Honest" begins with a silent "h" (vowel sound), so it takes "An." So "An honest officer."
questions.trick: Article choice follows SOUND, not spelling: an honest man, a university, an hour.

questions.question:
Find the segment that contains an error. If there is none, choose "No error".

If I was you, / I would accept / the transfer to / the head office.
questions.solution: In a hypothetical / unreal condition, use the subjunctive "were" for all subjects. So "If I were you."
questions.trick: For imaginary "if" statements, always use "were": If I were you / If he were rich.

questions.question:
Find the segment that contains an error. If there is none, choose "No error".

The scenery of Kashmir / are so beautiful / that tourists visit / it every season.
questions.solution: "Scenery" is an uncountable singular noun, so it takes a singular verb "is." So "The scenery ... is so beautiful."
questions.trick: Scenery, furniture, luggage, information — all uncountable, all singular.

questions.question:
Find the segment that contains an error. If there is none, choose "No error".

She returned back / from the training / programme earlier / than we expected.
questions.solution: Redundancy: "return" already means "come back," so "returned back" is repetitive. Use "She returned."
questions.trick: Cut the redundant "back" after return, revert, repeat, refer.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best replaces the marked part. If the original is correct, choose "No improvement".

The bank has decided to **do away the** outdated ledger system next quarter.
questions.solution: The phrasal verb is "do away WITH" (to abolish). It always needs "with."
questions.trick: Learn the fixed particle: do away WITH = abolish.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best replaces the marked part. If the original is correct, choose "No improvement".

Scarcely had the results been announced **than** the candidates began celebrating.
questions.solution: "Scarcely ... when" is the correct correlative (like Hardly ... when). "Than" is wrong here.
questions.trick: Scarcely/Hardly = WHEN. Only "No sooner" takes "than."

questions.question:
Choose the option that best replaces the marked part. If the original is correct, choose "No improvement".

If he **would have studied** the guidelines carefully, he would not have made the error.
questions.solution: Third conditional: "If + had + V3, ... would have + V3." Never use "would have" in the if-clause.
questions.trick: No "would" inside the "if" half of a conditional. If-clause takes "had + V3."

questions.question:
Choose the option that best replaces the marked part. If the original is correct, choose "No improvement".

The new recruit is **more efficient than any** employee in the team.
questions.solution: When comparing one member with the rest of its own group, add "other." Without it, the sentence illogically compares him to himself.
questions.trick: Comparative + "than any" within the same group needs "any OTHER."

questions.question:
Choose the option that best replaces the marked part. If the original is correct, choose "No improvement".

She is **senior than me** by three years in the organisation.
questions.solution: Latin comparatives (senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior, preferable) take "to," not "than."
questions.trick: Senior/junior/superior/inferior always pair with TO.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best replaces the marked part. If the original is correct, choose "No improvement".

Neither the auditor nor the accountants **has signed** the final statement yet.
questions.solution: With "neither ... nor," the verb agrees with the nearer subject "the accountants" (plural). So "have signed."
questions.trick: Nor's verb follows the nearest noun — here plural "accountants."

questions.question:
Choose the option that best replaces the marked part. If the original is correct, choose "No improvement".

No sooner did the alarm ring **when** everyone rushed to the exit.
questions.solution: "No sooner ... than" is the fixed pair. "When" is wrong.
questions.trick: No sooner = THAN (not when).

questions.question:
Choose the option that best replaces the marked part. If the original is correct, choose "No improvement".

The manager insisted **on me to complete** the report by evening.
questions.solution: "Insist" is not followed by "on + object + to-infinitive." Use "insist that + subject + base verb" (subjunctive). So "insisted that I complete."
questions.trick: Insist / demand / suggest + THAT + base verb.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best replaces the marked part. If the original is correct, choose "No improvement".

He **prefers coffee than tea** during the morning shift.
questions.solution: "Prefer" takes "to," not "than," when comparing two nouns.
questions.trick: Prefer X TO Y.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best replaces the marked part. If the original is correct, choose "No improvement".

The students were asked to **write down their names in capital letters** on the answer sheet.
options: write their names down in capitals letters
write down their name in capital letter
write down their names in capitals letter
writing down their names in capital letters
questions.solution: "Write down their names in capital letters" is already correct: plural "names" for plural students, and "capital letters" is the standard phrase.
questions.trick: Don't over-correct. If subject-verb, number and idiom all fit, keep the original.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best replaces the marked part. If the original is correct, choose "No improvement".

Being a rainy day, **the match was called off** by the organisers.
options: the organisers called off the match
questions.solution: Dangling modifier: "Being a rainy day" wrongly attaches to "the match," which cannot be a rainy day. The main clause needs a logical doer, so "the organisers called off the match" reads best of the options.
questions.trick: An opening participial phrase must describe the subject right after it. Fix a dangler by giving the main clause a real doer.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best replaces the marked part. If the original is correct, choose "No improvement".

He is **too weak to walking** without support after the surgery.
questions.solution: "Too + adjective + to + base verb." So "too weak to walk," not "to walking."
questions.trick: After "too ... to," use the plain (base) verb.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best replaces the marked part. If the original is correct, choose "No improvement".

The reason for his failure **is because he was** overconfident.
questions.solution: "The reason is because" is redundant (reason + because both give cause). Use "The reason is that."
questions.trick: Never write "reason is because" — replace with "reason is that."

questions.question:
Choose the option that best replaces the marked part. If the original is correct, choose "No improvement".

One should keep **his promises** if one wishes to be trusted.
questions.solution: The pronoun must agree with "one"; the correct possessive is "one's."
questions.trick: Start with "one," continue with "one's" — don't switch to "his" or "their."

questions.question:
Choose the option that best replaces the marked part. If the original is correct, choose "No improvement".

The higher you climb, **the coldest it becomes** on the mountain.
questions.solution: Parallel comparative structure: "The + comparative ..., the + comparative ..." So "The higher ..., the colder ..." — use the comparative, not the superlative "coldest."
questions.trick: In "The more ..., the more ..." sentences both blanks take the COMPARATIVE form.

questions.group: Part C — Word Swap / Usage & Confusables
questions.question:
Two words in the sentence have been interchanged and must be swapped back for it to make sense. Identify the pair.

The **principle** of the college addressed the students on the importance of moral **principal**.
questions.solution: "Principal" = head of a college (noun/person); "principle" = a moral rule. They are swapped. Correct: "The principal ... importance of moral principles."
questions.trick: The princiPAL is your PAL (the head person). PrinciplE = rulE.

questions.group: Part C — Word Swap / Usage & Confusables
questions.question:
Two words in the sentence have been interchanged and must be swapped back for it to make sense. Identify the pair.

The medicine had little **affect** on the patient, but the news deeply **effected** her mood.
questions.solution: "Affect" is the verb (to influence); "effect" as a noun means result. Correct: "little effect on the patient, but the news deeply affected her mood."
questions.trick: RAVEN — Affect = Verb; Effect = Noun. So use "effect" (noun) after "little," and "affected" (verb) as the action on her mood.

questions.group: Part C — Word Swap / Usage & Confusables
questions.question:
Two words in the sentence have been interchanged and must be swapped back for it to make sense. Identify the pair.

The manager gave his **council** on the matter, and the local **counsel** met to discuss the roads.
questions.solution: "Counsel" = advice / to advise; "council" = an assembly/body. Correct: "gave his counsel ... the local council met."
questions.trick: CounCIL = a Committee (people). CounSEL = adviSE / a lawyer.

questions.group: Part C — Word Swap / Usage & Confusables
questions.question:
Two words in the sentence have been interchanged and must be swapped back for it to make sense. Identify the pair.

The soldiers were **complimented** with rations, and the officer **supplemented** them on their bravery.
questions.solution: "Supplement" = to add to (rations); "compliment" = to praise (bravery). Correct: "soldiers were supplemented with rations ... officer complimented them on their bravery."
questions.trick: ComplIment = praIse. Supplement = supply extra.

questions.group: Part C — Word Swap / Usage & Confusables
questions.question:
Two words in the sentence have been interchanged and must be swapped back for it to make sense. Identify the pair.

He was careful not to **loose** his wallet, and the belt felt too **lose** around his waist.
questions.solution: "Lose" (verb) = fail to keep / misplace; "loose" (adjective) = not tight. They are swapped. Correct: "careful not to lose his wallet, and the belt felt too loose."
questions.trick: LOOSE rhymes with goose (adjective, extra o = extra slack). LOSE has one o — you "lost" an o. Verb of misplacing = lose.

questions.group: Part C — Word Swap / Usage & Confusables
questions.question:
Two words in the sentence have been interchanged and must be swapped back for it to make sense. Identify the pair.

The lawyer will **prosecute** the project next year, while the engineers **execute** the fraud case.
questions.solution: "Execute" = carry out (a project); "prosecute" = take legal action (a case). Correct: "engineers execute the project ... lawyer will prosecute the fraud case."
questions.trick: exeCUTE = carry out a plan. proseCUTE = pursue in court.

questions.group: Part C — Word Swap / Usage & Confusables
questions.question:
Two words in the sentence have been interchanged and must be swapped back for it to make sense. Identify the pair.

The storm will **adverse** affect the crops grown in this **adversely** low-lying region.
questions.solution: "Adversely" (adverb) must modify the verb "affect"; "adverse" (adjective) must modify the noun "region." They are swapped. Correct: "will adversely affect the crops grown in this adverse low-lying region."
questions.trick: Adverb before a verb: "adversely affect." Adjective before a noun: "adverse effect / adverse region."

questions.group: Part C — Word Swap / Usage & Confusables
questions.question:
Choose the correct word for the blank.

The committee will **______** the new policy at its next sitting.
questions.solution: "Adopt" = to take up / accept formally (a policy). "Adapt" = to adjust; "adept" = skilled.
questions.trick: adOPT = OPT to accept. adAPT = Adjust.

questions.group: Part C — Word Swap / Usage & Confusables
questions.question:
Choose the correct word for the blank.

Your careless remark may **______** his decision to resign.
questions.solution: Here we need a verb meaning "to influence" — "affect." "Effect" as a verb means "to bring about," which is not the sense here.
questions.trick: Verb slot after "may" means Affect (the Verb of the pair).

questions.group: Part C — Word Swap / Usage & Confusables
questions.question:
Choose the correct word for the blank.

The two ministers reached a **______** agreement on the trade issue.
questions.solution: "Mutual" = shared between both parties. "Neutral" = impartial; "moral" = ethical.
questions.trick: MUTUAL = shared by BOTH.

questions.group: Part C — Word Swap / Usage & Confusables
questions.question:
Choose the correct word for the blank.

He was **______** to the club after paying the annual fee.
questions.solution: "Admit to" = allow to enter/join. "Omit" = leave out; "emit" = give off; "submit" = hand in.
questions.trick: adMITted = let IN.

questions.group: Part C — Word Swap / Usage & Confusables
questions.question:
Choose the correct word for the blank.

The witness gave a **______** account of the accident to the police.
questions.solution: "Credible" = believable (the account). "Creditable" = praiseworthy; "credulous" = gullible (a person).
questions.trick: CredIBLE = believABLE. Creditable = deserves credit. Credulous = too trusting.

questions.group: Part C — Word Swap / Usage & Confusables
questions.question:
Choose the correct word for the blank.

The company decided to **______** its losses by cutting travel costs.
questions.solution: "Minimise" = reduce to the least (losses). The others are unrelated in meaning.
questions.trick: miniMISE = make the MINIMUM.

questions.group: Part C — Word Swap / Usage & Confusables
questions.question:
Choose the correct word for the blank.

Please **______** from smoking inside the office premises.
questions.solution: "Refrain from" = hold yourself back from an action. "Restrain" needs an object (restrain someone); the idiom for stopping oneself from doing something is "refrain from."
questions.trick: reFRAIN FROM doing. reSTRAIN someone/something.

questions.group: Part C — Word Swap / Usage & Confusables
questions.question:
Choose the correct word for the blank.

The new bridge will **______** the two districts across the river.
questions.solution: "Connect" = join two things (districts). "Collect," "correct," "collate," "convict" don't fit.
questions.trick: conNECT = join (think of a NETwork linking points).
